Chapter 6: Rethinking Schools — From Compliance to Curiosity
Picture this for a moment. There’s a teacher at the front of the classroom, handing out points for right answers, maybe giving warnings if homework’s missing. The students? Their eyes are glued to the scoreboard, because that’s what really counts in their minds.
But now, imagine a totally different scene. This time, the teacher’s sitting with the students, not above them. They’re asking, “What are you curious about today?” And together, they’re shaping what the lesson will look like. The room just feels different—less tense, way more alive.
For a lot of teachers, the thought of ditching rewards and punishments can be a little scary. I mean, isn’t that just asking for chaos? But here’s the thing—schools that have tried this approach have discovered some pretty surprising results.
Take one principal, for example. She was fed up with endless detentions and sticker charts, so she decided to shake things up. She encouraged teachers to focus on building real relationships and to give students more of a say in their own learning. Sure, the beginning was rocky—students pushed the limits, and teachers worried about losing control. But guess what happened over time?
Everything started to shift. Students stepped up, taking responsibility not just for their own work, but for the classroom community as a whole. They started asking better questions, taking more risks, and helping each other learn. Suddenly, the energy in the room changed.
In these kinds of classrooms, making mistakes isn’t something to be afraid of—it’s just part of learning. If a student’s struggling, the teacher doesn’t dangle a prize or threaten a penalty. Instead, they might ask, “What do you think would help?” or, “How can we figure this out together?” The whole focus moves away from just getting the right answer, and turns into exploring and solving problems together.
Students start trusting themselves and each other more. They don’t need constant pushing or pulling—they’re already motivated, because they’re curious and they feel like they belong. The teacher isn’t the enforcer anymore, but a guide, a partner in learning. Suddenly, the classroom becomes a place where learning is something you want to do, not something that’s forced on you.
And here’s something most folks don’t realize: the structure of school itself has a huge impact on motivation. When it’s all about grades, prizes, and punishments, students just learn to play the game. But when you shift the focus to questions, exploration, and working together, kids start to love learning for its own sake. It’s a subtle change—but it makes all the difference.
The real challenge isn’t just getting rid of rewards and punishments. It’s about building something better in their place. That means creating classrooms where students have real choices, where their voices matter, and where making mistakes is just another step along the way.
It’s about trusting students to care about their own learning, and supporting them as they figure out what really matters to them.
